quick: 1 g IM or IV daily for 60-120 days, then 1 g 2-3 times weekly (max 20 mg/kg/day)
Teratogenic in animals; use only if benefit outweighs risk (former Category C)
Excretion in human milk unknown - use with caution
Reduce dose - renally eliminated; high nephrotoxicity risk
No specific adjustment; use with caution
Avoid - added hepatic and adherence concerns
Renal function, audiometry, electrolytes (K/Mg/Ca), liver function
summary: Capreomycin is an injectable cyclic polypeptide antibiotic used as a second-line agent for tuberculosis caused by capreomycin-susceptible strains when first-line drugs have failed or cannot be used. It must always be given with other anti-TB agents. Its major toxicities - nephrotoxicity and cranial nerve VIII (auditory/vestibular) damage - parallel those of aminoglycosides and require close monitoring, especially in renal impairment or pre-existing hearing loss.
indications: Pulmonary tuberculosis caused by capreomycin-susceptible strains of M. tuberculosis, used concomitantly with other antituberculosis agents, when primary agents (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, aminosalicylic acid, streptomycin) are ineffective or cannot be used due to toxicity or resistance

dosage.d: 1 g daily (not exceeding 20 mg/kg/day) IM or IV
Reduce dose based on creatinine clearance

admin: Reconstitute the 1 g vial with 2 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride or Sterile Water for Injection; allow 2-3 minutes for complete dissolution
For IV use, dilute reconstituted solution in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride and infuse over 60 minutes
For IM use, give by deep injection into a large muscle mass (superficial injection causes pain and sterile abscess)
Always use concomitantly with other antituberculosis agents
moa: Capreomycin is a cyclic polypeptide antibiotic that inhibits mycobacterial protein synthesis by acting on the ribosome (binding to the 70S ribosome/interfering with translation). It is bacteriostatic against M. tuberculosis. The precise molecular target overlaps with other ribosomally active agents, contributing to cross-resistance with viomycin and partial cross-resistance with aminoglycosides such as kanamycin/amikacin.

relative: Concurrent use with other ototoxic/nephrotoxic drugs (streptomycin, viomycin, aminoglycosides, polymyxins, colistin, vancomycin)

preg: Capreomycin has been shown to be teratogenic in rats at multiples of the human dose; there are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women (formerly Pregnancy Category C). Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether capreomycin is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk, exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: Capreomycin is excreted by the kidneys and is markedly nephrotoxic; use in renal insufficiency only with great caution. Reduce the dose based on creatinine clearance and monitor renal function frequently. Accumulation in renal impairment increases the risk of further renal and eighth-nerve toxicity.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is established. Monitor liver function periodically, especially when combined with other potentially hepatotoxic anti-TB drugs.

major: Aminoglycosides (streptomycin, amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin, kanamycin, neomycin) - additive nephro/ototoxicity
Viomycin - similar irreversible eighth-nerve and renal toxicity (avoid concurrent use)
Polymyxin A, colistin, vancomycin - additive nephrotoxic/ototoxic potential
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - hepatic burden and adherence concerns
interactions.diagnostics: Can elevate BUN/creatinine and lower serum potassium, magnesium, and calcium

common: Pain, induration, and bleeding at injection sites
rare: Neuromuscular blockade with respiratory depression (high doses)
emergency: Sudden severe hearing or vestibular loss

monitoring: Renal function (BUN, serum creatinine, creatinine clearance) and urinalysis at baseline and regularly
Audiometric and vestibular testing at baseline and during therapy
counsel: This injection treats tuberculosis and must be combined with your other TB medicines - never use it alone
Report any hearing changes, ringing in the ears, dizziness, or balance problems immediately
Report reduced urination, swelling, or unusual fatigue
Regular blood tests and hearing checks are required during treatment
Complete the full course exactly as prescribed to prevent resistance
pk: Antimycobacterial activity follows absorption; clinical TB response is gradual over weeks
Peak serum concentration about 1-2 hours after IM injection
Approximately 3-6 hours (markedly prolonged in renal impairment)
Reconstituted solution may be stored up to 48 hours refrigerated; store powder per labeling, protect from light
pearls: Capreomycin IS FDA-approved (Capastat Sulfate) - a second-line injectable for MDR-TB
Toxicity profile (nephro- and ototoxicity, electrolyte wasting) mirrors aminoglycosides - monitor kidneys, hearing, and electrolytes
Avoid concurrent aminoglycosides/viomycin and other oto/nephrotoxic drugs - additive cranial nerve VIII and renal injury
Cross-resistance with kanamycin/amikacin and viomycin can occur
missed: If a scheduled injection is missed, contact the TB treatment provider promptly to reschedule; do not double a dose. Consistent administration with the full multidrug regimen is essential to prevent resistance.
overdose: Overdose intensifies nephrotoxicity, eighth-nerve toxicity, electrolyte loss (hypokalemia), and may potentiate neuromuscular blockade with respiratory depression. Management is supportive: maintain hydration and renal perfusion, correct electrolyte abnormalities, provide respiratory support if neuromuscular blockade occurs, and use hemodialysis to enhance removal in severe cases or renal failure.
